headline: Trump Calls Huang to Assure Markets That AI Won't Kill Us
subheadline: A sitting president and the world's most powerful chip CEO jointly dismiss existential risk onstage, proving either confidence in AI safety or confidence in regulatory capture.
source_headline: Trump and Jensen Huang unite against AI doomers in surprise on-stage call
body_html:
On Monday at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, President Trump called into the stage where Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was speaking to jointly dismiss concerns about AI existential risk. The appearance—a surprise call, we're told, because nothing says spontaneous like coordinating a presidential phone call during a live event—marked a clear political and business alliance against what both men characterized as "AI doomerism." This is either the most reassuring moment in technology policy, or the most clarifying display of how capital and political power align when there's money to be made.

For context: Nvidia manufactures the GPUs that power every major AI system on Earth. The company's valuation has been turbocharged by the generative AI boom, making it arguably the most foundational business in the entire AI stack. Huang controls the infrastructure that enables the very capabilities that some scientists and ethicists worry about. Trump, now a sitting president, is using his platform to tell markets and voters that those worries are overblown. The dynamics here are so clean they seem almost designed for a regulatory capture case study.

The All-In Summit itself is a gathering of venture capitalists and tech entrepreneurs who have collectively bet trillions that AI will be transformative and profitable. The audience is not neutral. It is composed of people whose personal wealth is directly tied to AI adoption accelerating without friction—regulatory, legislative, or existential. Huang has appeared at this summit before; Trump's involvement is new. But the message is consistent: trust us, trust growth, dismiss the doubters.

The framing of "AI doomerism" is worth examining. It's not a neutral term; it's a rhetorical move that conflates legitimate safety concerns with irrational panic. The people raising questions about AI alignment, concentration of power, or systemic risk are not necessarily claiming that superintelligent systems will immediately exterminate humanity tomorrow. Many are asking whether we should ship transformative technology without understanding it, and whether the people building it have sufficient accountability. But calling that "doomerism" lets you dismiss it without engaging with it—a rhetorical move made vastly more powerful when it comes from the president.

What could go wrong? Consider the precedent. A sitting executive and a sitting president have now jointly signaled to regulators, the press, and the market that skepticism about AI risk is not legitimate policy concern—it's obstruction. That signal matters when antitrust cases are being evaluated, when export restrictions on chips are being written, or when international AI governance frameworks are being negotiated. Huang doesn't need explicit favors; the message itself is the favor.

This moment crystallizes something larger about the current VC and tech moment: the industry's relationship with power has become explicit rather than implicit. Venture capital no longer lobbies around policy—it coordinates directly with it, onstage, in real time, with no intermediary. The fact that this happened at a private summit full of LPs and founders, not at a public hearing or congressional testimony, makes the point even clearer. This is how business gets done now.

In five years, either this call will have been the moment wisdom and humility prevailed over irrational fear, or it will have been the moment two powerful men assured the world that their trillion-dollar bet on AI wouldn't need to slow down for anyone's concerns—including their own.
glossary_definition: Any criticism of AI deployment, safety, or concentration of power that can be dismissed by calling whoever raised it irrational, thus eliminating the need to actually engage with the argument.
